input:
The pressure drop arising from friction in a horizontal pipe is one of the most fundamental calculations in fluid mechanics, and it is evaluated here for water flowing under a representative set of conditions. Water at 293 K has a density $\rho$ of 998 kg m-3, and it flows through the pipe at a mean velocity $v$ of 1.2 m s-1. The pipe has a diameter $D$ of 0.1 m and a length $L$ of 115 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ for the conditions in question is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is calculated from the Darcy-Weisbach relation, in which $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop, $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the pipe length, $D$ is the pipe diameter, $\rho$ is the fluid density and $v$ is the mean velocity:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

Substitution of the stated values into this relation gives a friction pressure drop of 16.5 kPa, which is the pressure that a pump or other driving device must supply merely in order to overcome friction along this length of pipe, over and above any pressure required for elevation changes or for the process itself. Because the pipe is horizontal, no allowance for static head is required in this particular calculation, and because the velocity enters the relation as a square, it follows that even modest increases in the flow rate, and hence in the mean velocity, will produce disproportionately large increases in the friction loss, a point that is well worth bearing in mind when operating conditions are changed. The result is of course sensitive to the friction factor adopted, and the value used here should be understood as the value appropriate to the stated conditions rather than as a universal constant for water flowing in pipes.
target:
Calculate the friction pressure drop for water in a horizontal pipe. Water at 293 K (density $\rho$ = 998 kg m-3) flows at a mean velocity $v$ of 1.2 m s-1 in a pipe of diameter $D$ = 0.1 m and length $L$ = 115 m; the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The pipe is horizontal, so no static-head term enters the calculation, and the density is constant along the length. The friction pressure drop is calculated from the Darcy-Weisbach relation

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop, $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the pipe length, $D$ is the pipe diameter, $\rho$ is the density and $v$ is the mean velocity. The relation gives $\Delta P$ = 16.5 kPa. The velocity term governs the sensitivity of the result: $\Delta P$ varies with the square of $v$, so a rise in flow rate raises the friction loss in proportion to the square of that rise, and the pump duty set from the stated figure must be revisited if the operating flow changes. The friction factor carries the remaining uncertainty. The value used is the value at the stated conditions; a rougher pipe wall, or a lower Reynolds number in a colder stream, raises $f$ and raises the pressure drop in direct proportion. The result is the friction loss for the stated pipe and conditions alone, and fittings, valves and entrance and exit losses are not included in it. In a pump calculation, the friction loss stands alongside the static lift and the pressure difference between the suction and delivery vessels, and the three are added before the pump head is fixed; the stated figure supplies only the first of the three, and a pump selected on the friction figure alone would be undersized for any duty that also lifts the liquid or delivers it against pressure. The length dependence is linear, so the figure scales to a revised routing in direct proportion to the added length, provided the diameter and the velocity are unchanged.
